title: Flow Mismatching: Unsupervised Anomaly Detection via Velocity Discrepancies in Flow Matching Models
claim: Learned normal dynamics agree with the geometric path toward normal targets but diverge for anomalous ones, exposing an anomaly signal.
layout: Single (x,t) plot, bottom-to-top time, colored paths with arrows at selected times
description: A single 2-D toy plot with data coordinate x on the horizontal axis (-3 to 4) and time t on the vertical axis (0 to 1). A blue Gaussian density bump at the bottom (t=0) stands for the prior. A peach, multi-modal density at the top (t=1) stands for normal data. Faint gray arrows point mostly upward and form the learned flow field. Thin blue curves are flow trajectories. Two thick straight affine paths start at the same black point at x=0, t=0. The green path ends at a normal sample at x≈1.5, t=1. The red path ends at an anomalous sample at x≈-2.5, t=1. Dots mark selected times on each path. At each dot, a blue arrow shows the model-predicted velocity and a colored arrow shows the geometric velocity. On the green path the two arrows align. On the red path they visibly diverge. The eye goes first to the red and green diagonals.
caption: Velocity mismatch in the (x, t) plane. Light arrows denote the learned flow vθ(x, t) from prior to normal data, while colored affine paths from the same x0 target either a normal sample (green) or an anomalous sample (red). At selected times, the predicted velocity vθ(xt, t) aligns with the geometric velocity y −x0 for normal targets but disagrees for anomalous targets, revealing the anomaly signal.
abstract: We propose Flow Mismatching, an unsupervised anomaly detection method that deliberately avoids reconstruction-based paradigms. Instead, we treat flow matching as geometric dynamics and leverage a key insight: anomalies occur at places where the learned normal flow disagrees with the geometric path toward a test image. Given a flow matching model trained only on normal images, we probe its learned velocity field along affine paths from Gaussian noise to a target image. Along each path, we compare the model-predicted velocity, which follows normal generative dynamics, with the geometric velocity toward the target, which includes any anomalous content. Anomalies induce strong local disagreement between these velocities. Aggregating the mismatch over different time steps and multiple paths yields pixel-wise heatmaps and image-level scores without test-time optimization, feature memories, or additional calibration. Our analysis shows that the population mismatch decomposes into an irreducible denoising term and a Fisher-divergence term between the test-path and normal-path score functions, which identifies the score-gap component that drives anomaly separation and explains the effectiveness of robust path aggregation. Extensive experiments on MVTec-AD and VisA demonstrate competitive performance compared with established reconstruction-based and recent flow matching-based approaches.
